zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical review aid: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Consulted after independent scan reading; the diplomatic readings and English notes here are reviewer-authored, not an imported transcription.

runs.text: Nem entendia o que lhe falauão.

lines.note: Translates the quotation at the end of the preceding page: the person did not understand what was said to him. Nem is running text here, not a second catchword.
Fushigi na koto explains a strange or extraordinary matter. The Portuguese causar is divided at the line end.

runs.text: ſa eſpanto, ou duuida. ¶ Item, Couſa que

lines.note: Completes the sense of causing astonishment or doubt and begins a further explanation involving personal unease.

runs.text: toca de que hum ſe toma, ou deſconfia, &c.

lines.note: Continues the source's wording about something that affects a person or arouses distrust. Deſconfia has f, not the OCR's long s; the unusual toca wording is not rewritten.
Kira concerns brightness or splendor. The example begins Qira- in roman type; the draft's italic O was a misread Q.
Completes kira wo migaku furumai, explained as an impressive feast or entertainment; the Portuguese qualification continues below.

Finishes the feast gloss and gives a phrase for splendid attire. The scan appears to read nigaita, although the preceding migaqu and the sense suggest migaita; the apparent printed n is retained provisionally.
Translates the preceding phrase as splendid dress. The provisional st allograph is retained without a global typography substitution.
A separate kira entry describes a kind of fine fabric or textile piece, not the preceding abstract splendor.
Kirabiyakana means bright or splendid. The example repeats the adjective across the physical line break.
Describes a splendidly presented group of people, with the Portuguese adverb continuing on the following row.
Completes lustrosamente and explains that the people are splendidly dressed.
Miyako e kaeru explains a return to the capital. The Portuguese place-name is deferred to the next physical row.
Miyaco completes the Portuguese return-to-capital gloss. Although alone on this row, it belongs within that explanation and qualifies for whole-word typeface review.
This kirai entry concerns hunger coming upon someone, distinct from the following dislike verb.
The example pairs becoming hungry with eating, explicitly confirmed by the Portuguese translation.
Gives the principal forms of kirau, to dislike or reject. The two abbreviated endings carry carons.
Gives the corresponding noun for aversion or refusal, separately from the inflected verb above.
Kirameki means shining or gleaming. The damaged opening character is Q rather than OCR G, consistent with the visible neighboring initials.

runs.text: liſo, & nedeo como couſa bem vruxada.

lines.note: Specifies a smooth, sleek surface like a well-burnished object. The unusual historical vruxada is preserved.
Names an herb without further description. No modern species identification is inserted into the transcription or gloss.
Describes soft clothing made of fine materials; the long compound is retained with its printed final-u caron.

runs.text: & de pelles, ou lãa branda, & molle.

lines.note: Adds skins or soft wool as materials, retaining the printed lãa and doubled l of molle.
Describes rich silk clothing and other luxurious fabrics. The Portuguese outras begins across the line break.
Completes outras and gives brocade-like fabric as an example of the rich materials.
Kirakirato is an adverb describing sparkling. The Portuguese reads Modo, not the OCR's Medo; Adu. is italic apparatus.
Completes the description as shining or gleaming from a distance.

runs.text: Hũa laya de criſtal que ſe tira ẽ algũs

lines.note: Kirara is described as a crystal-like substance obtained from mountains. The abbreviated ẽ and algũs are preserved without expansion.

runs.text: montes, mas mais brando, & facil de diuidir q̃

lines.note: Distinguishes the material as softer and easier to divide than ordinary crystal; the comparison continues below.
Finishes the mineral comparison. The source's physical description is retained rather than replaced by a modern mineral name.
Kiratame means judging or discerning. The scan supports Iulgar and diſcernir, correcting two letter losses or confusions in the draft.
Begins a polite request to examine or settle the matter thoroughly. The honorific request ending is divided after cudaſa-.

runs.text: Peço vos que tireis iſto alimpo, & o a-

lines.note: Completes kudasarei; the Portuguese asks for clarification. Peço and tireis replace OCR Pego and tirets, while alimpo remains attached as printed.
Completes aclareis, finishing the request to clarify the matter.
Kireru is defined through a thread or cord breaking. Corda corrects the OCR's conda.
Introduces the metaphorical expression naka ga kiruru: a relationship breaks off. The Portuguese object follows below.
Completes the broken-friendship example, then introduces a horse veering away. The Portuguese desviar-se is physically divided.

runs.text: arſe o caualo do caminho eſpantandoſe, quando

lines.note: Explains that the horse leaves the path when startled, with the circumstances continued below.
Specifies a running or walking horse and starts the Japanese example, dividing uma after its initial v.
Completes kono uma wa kireyasui uma ja, a horse prone to shying. Maua and qireyaſui correct OCR mana and qiteyaſui.
Describes the horse as skittish and liable to veer or leap aside easily.
Completes the example by specifying movement off the path.
A separate kireru entry concerns chapping or cracking of feet and hands. The source has pees with two e types.

runs.text: &c, com frio. ¶ Item, Ser cortado com

lines.note: Attributes the cracking to cold, then adds the sense of being cut by a weapon.
Catana completes the Portuguese explanation of being cut by a sword; it is not a new Japanese headword.
Defines the cutting effectiveness of a knife or razor. Cortar replaces OCR Certar, and the headword is restored to flush-left placement.
Kono kamisori wa kirenu says these razors do not cut. The negative qirenu and the preceding word boundary replace the garbled OCR; the translation continues in column 2.

runs.text: lhas não cortam, ou rapam mal.

lines.note: Completes naualhas from column 1: the razors do not cut or shave poorly. This continuation remains at the top of column 2.
Kire is a small piece of anything, a noun distinct from the preceding cutting verbs.
The reduplicated kiregire is glossed as small pieces in the plural.
Isagiyoi koto explains cleanness or purity. The opening Q corrects OCR D without changing the printed Japanese synonym.
Gives the adjectival form kireina, describing a clean thing.
Supplies the associated adverbial form kireini. The scan has no separate Portuguese gloss on this indented row, so none is invented.
Supplies the abstract-noun form kireisa, again without a printed gloss. The short indented row is intentional, not omitted text.

runs.text: Souela, ou furador, ou verruma de

lines.note: Kiri is an awl or boring tool. The enlarged tool-name has two r types followed by u and m: verruma, rather than the OCR's veruna.
Completes the description of the Japanese boring tool. Iapão is Portuguese and is not marked as an embedded Japanese expression.
A separate kiri means mist or fine rain. Chuua has two u types, correcting the draft's chua.
Gives kiru, to cut, and the compound yomi kiru. The initial Q replaces OCR G; the example is explained on the following row.

runs.text: Ler atè certo lugar, & não ir por diante.

lines.note: Explains reading up to a particular point and not continuing beyond it, preserving this historical sense of the compound.
Fude wo kakikiru is using up the writing implement through writing. The Portuguese object continues below.
Completes the writing example and introduces saying something decisively. Eſcreuer corrects the OCR's final a; Iyqiru retains its printed joined form.

runs.text: Dizer reſolutamente. E geralmente eſte verbo

lines.note: Translates the speech example as speaking resolutely, then begins an explicit general explanation of compound kiru.

runs.text: junto com a raiz de outros ſignifica fazerſe de

lines.note: States that attaching this verb to another verb's stem can indicate a complete action; the qualification continues below.

runs.text: todo, ou acabarſe perfeitamente algũa couſa.

lines.note: Completes the grammatical explanation as doing something wholly or finishing it perfectly.
Kiriai denotes exchanging sword blows. The Portuguese pelejando begins at the physical line edge.

runs.text: lejando hũs com os outros na batalha, &c.

lines.note: Completes the description of fighting one another in battle. Pelejando and batalha correct OCR vowel and consonant confusions.
Kiriame denotes fine rain or drizzle; the short entry stands independently between cutting compounds.
Kiriake means opening by cutting. The example begins michi, road, divided across rows.
Completes michi and gives an alternative road-word before kiriakuru. The Portuguese mato begins after the Japanese example, without a supplied hyphen.
To completes Portuguese mato, brushwood, not a Japanese word. The entire row is italic: clearing brush or herbs opens a path.
Kiriawase concerns equalizing or fitting things together by cutting; the Portuguese alternative continues below.
Completes the joining sense. The descender of j is visible in ajuntar, correcting OCR auntar.

runs.text: Trincho, ou taboa ſobre que cortão o

lines.note: Kiriban is a chopping board, described as the board on which food is cut.
Completes the description as preparing food away from the dining table. Fora has f rather than the draft's long s.
Kirikakari means rushing at someone with a cutting attack; the Portuguese object follows below.
Completes the attack gloss and begins teki ni kirikakaru, striking at an enemy.
Completes the divided verb kirikakaru. This short Japanese continuation has no independent Portuguese gloss.
Kirikachi is prevailing by force of arms. The initial syllable is Qiri, not the OCR's Quri.
Kirikami is a short written message or letter. The scan corrects the opening Q and the Portuguese words Eſcrito and carta.
Kirikake concerns cutting and placing something upon another surface. The initial Q replaces the OCR's G.
Gives earth as one material, then begins the separate example kubi wo kirikakuru, explained below.

runs.text: Cortando a cabeça dalguem pola, ou depen-

lines.note: Explains placing or hanging a severed head. The historical pola is retained without supplying a modern accent or hyphen.
Completes dependurala and specifies suspension from a pole or stick.
Kirikaeshi is striking back at someone who struck first. Tornar replaces the OCR's Ternar.
Completes the retaliation gloss and supplies the nominal construction kirigaeshi wo suru. The printed c/g alternation between headword and example is preserved.
Kirichirashi includes scattering or putting others to flight by cutting attacks. The Portuguese expression is divided after eſpa-.

runs.text: lha fato, ou fazer fugir. ¶ Item, Cortan-

lines.note: Completes the scattering expression and introduces the second sense of cutting material into scattered pieces.
Describes dispersing and breaking something into pieces by cutting. The attached empedaços is preserved.
Paper supplies an example of material cut into pieces; the short row completes the preceding clause.
Kirikoguchi is the cut end or edge of an object. The scan supports abbreviated Põta and cortada, replacing the garbled OCR Tta certada.
Kirikomi describes entering among enemies while striking. The two Portuguese nasal abbreviations and the absence of a final punctuation mark are retained.
Kirikoroshi is killing with a sword. The descender in eſpada identifies p, correcting the OCR's t.

runs.text: Ponta cortada: ou abertura q̃ fica

lines.note: Kirikuchi denotes a cut edge or the opening left by cutting. The initial and medial letters restore Qiricuchi from OCR Ginicuchi.

runs.text: em couſa, q̃ ſe começou acortar.

lines.note: Completes the definition as an opening in something that has begun to be cut. The source's attached acortar is preserved. The lower-right Qiri is a catchword; its narrow final i is undotted or worn, so that furniture reading is recorded as provisional.
